prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms

statement.case_for: B012 is the candidate on which this committee agrees most. Seven of eight members ranked it, two placed it first and three placed it in the top three, and all seven proposed the same two names. Scientifically it is a clean case of a new idea becoming a new regime of measurement. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping thousands of atoms in coherent interrogation, and Ye's group pushed the systematic uncertainty and stability to the 1e-18 level, including the many-body and collective effects. Several national laboratories now reproduce this performance and compare clocks over fibre links, and the field has gone from proof of principle to redefinition of the second being discussed. The scientific discovery, not only the application, is visible here: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of constants and a new class of quantum-coherent many-atom instrument. As a theorist I also value that this is an experiment where every physical detail (lattice light shifts, collisions, blackbody radiation) has been tracked down and understood. The two-person attribution is unusually clear for a modern experimental prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is lineage and novelty. The 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, trapped-ion control and ion clocks) already honour the technical ground on which lattice clocks stand, so the committee must be able to state what is distinct, namely the magic-wavelength neutral-atom lattice and many-atom interrogation. Credit for early demonstrations and systematics is also shared with groups such as Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley, and the ion-clock community (for example Al+ clocks) may feel left out. Finally, the headline promise, a redefinition of the second and relativistic geodesy, is still ahead of us, so this could be argued to reward a metrology instrument before its main application is realised. My own first choice, B051, is much thinner in support, and I should not equate my interest in it with committee-wide merit.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a textbook case of a measurement method that opens new observation, with 1e-18 uncertainties and a route to redefining the second, and he ranks circuit QED only sixth because of overlap with the recent 2025 circuit prize.
responses.response: I agree on B012 and have moved it to the top of my configuration. On circuit QED I also accept the substance of his overlap concern. The 2025 prize honoured macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a circuit, whereas cQED is a different discovery, light-matter strong coupling and dispersive readout on a chip, but a committee that awarded superconducting circuits last year will reasonably ask whether back-to-back recognition of the same platform is wise. I think the overlap is real enough to keep B051 as an alternative for a later year rather than my lead candidate, and I should say plainly that my enthusiasm is shaped by my own field.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B012 first, stressing that Katori's lattice idea is a clean, somewhat unexpected route to extreme precision that enables tests of constants and gravitational time dilation over millimetres, and she judges that a two-name prize is fair. She also ranks quantum-gate work with ions and atoms (B010) third.
responses.response: I share her reading of B012 and her view that the two-name configuration is fair, and her comment on the 2005 comb prize matches my own caveat. Where I would qualify is on B010: I rank it second, but the 2012 prize to Wineland already covers single trapped-ion control, and the 2022 prize covers entanglement tests, so Cirac, Zoller and Blatt would have to be justified as distinct achievements. I do not think that blocks it, but I would not pair it with B012 in a two-part prize because the allocation would exceed three people and dilute both citations.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators first for its universal bulk-edge mechanism, but flags that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who predicted the HgTe realisation, are not among the credited names, which is a real gap in a three-person prize.
responses.response: I agree with that gap, and it is the main reason I would not put B057 above B012 even though I rank it third on scientific grounds. The Kane-Mele theory and Molenkamp's HgTe measurement are decisive, but a prize that leaves out the HgTe prediction invites the question that the Kane-Mele paper is not the whole story, and the 2016 topological-phases prize reduces novelty further. I disagree mildly that this makes B057 the best lead: its credit problem is structurally harder than the clean attribution of B012.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing that a predicted flat-band condition was confirmed experimentally and opened correlated insulators and superconductivity in a clean, tunable platform, independently reproduced worldwide.
responses.response: I take the prediction-plus-confirmation argument seriously and the platform is remarkable, which is why I keep B036 near the top of my list. My reservation is maturity: the mechanism of the superconductivity is still unsettled, the field is only seven years old, and the experimental credit (Cao and collaborators, Dean's group) is wider than the three names supplied. B012 is more settled, so I would hold B036 for a few more years while the physics clarifies, rather than make it the lead now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that optical lattice clocks are a sufficiently distinct achievement from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes.
Whether other groups' contributions to the first strontium lattice clock demonstrations and systematics evaluations (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others) should alter the two-name credit.
Whether the second will actually be redefined on optical clocks, and whether the prize is then better timed after that decision.
How much weight the committee wants to give to a back-to-back superconducting-circuit prize if B051 or a related candidate advances.
statement.conflict_note: My own opening first choice, B051 (circuit QED), lies in my research field and I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, whose Chalmers colleagues work closely with superconducting-circuit groups, so I should consider recusal or at least defer to colleagues on B051. Quantum-computing platforms in B010 are adjacent to my WACQT role, so some caution applies there. No specific personal or institutional connection to B012 is apparent from my profile.
